what_it_does: A water-soluble vitamin B3 ingredient that supports the skin barrier, tone, texture, and oil balance.
summary_short: Niacinamide is a well-studied, generally well-tolerated ingredient for barrier support, uneven tone, redness, and signs of aging. A 5% niacinamide study found improvements in fine lines, dark spots, redness, sallowness, and elasticity after 12 weeks.
summary_long:
Niacinamide, also called nicotinamide, is a form of vitamin B3 used in skincare for barrier support, uneven tone, redness, texture, and visible signs of aging. It is water-soluble and works partly by supporting skin energy processes involving NAD and NADP, which are important for normal cell function [PMID:unknown].

For the skin barrier, niacinamide has been reported to reduce transepidermal water loss and improve moisture in the outer layer of skin. It may also support keratin production, ceramide synthesis, and healthy keratinocyte differentiation, which helps explain why it is often used in moisturizers and products for dry, sensitive, or compromised skin [PMID:unknown].

Clinical evidence is strongest for cosmetic benefits such as improved tone, redness, texture, and aging-related changes. In a 12-week split-face study, 5% niacinamide used twice daily improved fine lines and wrinkles, hyperpigmented spots, red blotchiness, yellowing, and elasticity compared with vehicle control [PMID:unknown]. Reviews also describe potential benefits for acne-prone skin, rosacea-prone skin, itching, dermatitis, and actinic keratosis, though the level of evidence varies by condition.

Niacinamide is generally considered well tolerated and safe in cosmetic use. Some people may still experience stinging, flushing, or irritation, especially with high-strength formulas or when the skin barrier is already irritated. For daily use, many consumer products use niacinamide around 2–5%, while 5% is a commonly studied level for visible tone and texture benefits.

Niacinamide pairs well with moisturizers, ceramides, hyaluronic acid, panthenol, retinoids, sunscreen, and many pigment-focused ingredients. It is often used alongside exfoliating acids or retinoids to help support barrier comfort, but very sensitive skin may prefer introducing those combinations slowly.
quick_facts: Can help uneven tone and redness
Pairs well with ceramides and retinoids
